messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Daniel Kraus was 45, a widowed military medic from a German-American family, and when he first came to treatment he spoke with the flattened precision of someone used to staying functional under pressure. The flood had struck the town where his unit had been deployed during a major disaster response, and he still described the night in fragments: the siren cutting out, the generator failing, water pushing through the streets, people shouting from dark windows, a child separated from her mother in the chaos. He had been moving from one trapped resident to another with his pack and stretcher when a collapsing wall sent a shock through the building and pinned part of the stairwell. In the months that followed, Daniel found that any sudden bang—a dropped tray in the supermarket, a backfiring engine outside his apartment, even a door slamming in the clinic—sent him instantly into high alert. At work in the military medical unit he watched every corridor and doorway, sat where he could see exits, and never quite let himself relax, even in places everyone else treated as safe.

The memory of the flood did not return to him as a tidy story. When it came, it came as terror, as if his body had been dropped back into the same night; he would stop mid-sentence, stare, and need time before he could continue. He said the scenes would not stay in order: the faces, the waterline, the shouting, the trapped stairwell, and the moment he realized he could not get to everyone. That confusion made the memory feel even more unbearable, and the more it overwhelmed him, the more he came to believe that something in him had broken beyond repair. He had once defined himself by being calm under fire, by knowing what to do when others panicked, and now he felt he no longer knew who he was. He told the clinician that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore, that the beliefs he had once lived by—that competence mattered, that suffering could be organized into service, that the world could still be made orderly through training and duty—had been shattered by what he had seen in the flood.

Those same beliefs about himself and the world then colored the memories when they arrived again. If the images rushed back while he was alone, he would think, with a grim certainty, that he had failed the people he was supposed to protect, and that he had become someone unrecognizable to himself. What had happened in the disaster seemed, in his mind, to prove that his old understanding of the world was false, and the memory became easier to summon in its emotional weight than in any coherent sequence. He would begin to replay the scene, not to make sense of it but to test where he had gone wrong, and each attempt left him more convinced that there was no stable meaning left to hold onto. The result was a narrowing of his life: he avoided news about storms, declined invitations that would take him near water, and kept himself busy with extra shifts because idleness made the recollections more likely to break through. At home, in the quiet apartment he now inhabited alone, the silence had become as hard to bear as the memories, and he would leave the television on just to cover the spaces in which his mind might drift back.

The body of the fear never fully stood down. Daniel remained keyed to sudden sound, scanning before he entered rooms, stiffening whenever footsteps echoed in the hallway outside his quarters. He knew, intellectually, that he was not back in the flood, but his body did not behave as if it believed him. The watchfulness fed his sense that the world was no longer trustworthy, and that conviction made it harder to settle when the memory returned, because each recall seemed to confirm that nothing had been restored. He spoke of going to sleep already braced for an alarm, of feeling unable to relax even after long, uneventful days, and of hating how quickly he now measured every environment for danger. As his fear of sounds and his constant guarding continued, he found himself more alone, more withdrawn from colleagues and friends, and more certain that the man his wife had known was gone. He had finally sought help after catching himself freezing in the medic station when a metal cart crashed in the corridor, his chest tight and his mind flooded with the flood again. What he most feared was that this was the rest of his life: that the terror, the disordered memories, and the sense of having lost both his purpose and his identity would never let him return to himself.
